overview: Cohort of all peripheral intravenous catheters inserted on adult medical and surgical wards from 1 March 2024 to 28 February 2026, comparing the 12 months after the change to clinically indicated replacement with the 12 months before, built from existing flowsheet and infection surveillance data.
population: Catheters inserted on adult medical and surgical wards in patients aged 18 and over; catheters inserted in the emergency department or operating theatres are excluded from the primary analysis and described separately; catheters without a removal record at discharge are counted and handled in a sensitivity analysis.
exposure: Insertion from 1 March 2025 to 28 February 2026 (after the change) versus 1 March 2024 to 28 February 2025 (before).
procedures: Clinical informatics extracts every eligible flowsheet record and links it to the admission episode and to the infection prevention surveillance list inside the hospital's secure environment; the analysis file carries study identifiers only. Removal reasons are mapped to failure (phlebitis, infiltration, occlusion, dislodgement) or non-failure (end of treatment, discharge, routine resite) with a coding rule fixed before extraction, because flowsheet reasons were missing for 11 percent of removals in a validation study (c6); a second nurse recodes a random 5 percent of free-text reasons. Co-interventions on the wards (staffing changes, new catheter products, education sessions) are listed by month from ward managers' records.

outcomes.name: Catheter failure
outcomes.measure: Removal for phlebitis, infiltration, occlusion or dislodgement before the end of treatment, per catheter
outcomes.why: Failure interrupts treatment and means another insertion; it is the harm ward nurses fear from longer dwell.

outcomes.name: Catheters per admission
outcomes.measure: Number of peripheral catheters inserted per admission episode
outcomes.why: The benefit the policy was meant to bring and the one patients notice.

outcomes.name: Peripheral catheter-associated bloodstream infection
outcomes.measure: Surveillance-confirmed infections, reported as counts and per 1,000 catheter-days without a test
outcomes.timing: During dwell and 48 hours after removal
outcomes.why: The executive's concern; too rare for a comparison but must be reported.

outcomes.name: Documentation completeness
outcomes.measure: Proportion of catheter shifts with a documented phlebitis score, by day, night and weekend, and proportion of removals with a coded reason
outcomes.timing: Every shift during dwell; at removal
outcomes.why: The policy relies on assessment every shift, and failure can only be measured where a reason is recorded.

feasibility: About 30 hours of clinical informatics time for extraction and linkage (request CI-2026-117); analysis by the investigator with a hospital statistician; results before June 2027.
biasMitigation: Failure coding rule fixed before extraction, with a 5 percent recode by a second nurse
Monthly time series with 12 points on each side and co-interventions annotated
Six covariates fixed before extraction; dwell time not adjusted for because it lies on the causal path of the policy

biasFlags.label: Secular trends and co-interventions
biasFlags.note: Two consecutive years differ in more than the policy; the time series and co-intervention list limit but do not remove this.

biasFlags.label: Documentation differing between periods
biasFlags.note: Removal reasons may have been recorded more carefully after the change; the recode and missing-reason sensitivity analysis check this.

biasFlags.label: Clustering of catheters within patients
biasFlags.note: Handled with a patient-level frailty term (claim c4).

flags: Bloodstream infection reported without a test
parsimony.simplestPath: One exposure contrast, one primary outcome, one clustered model and one pre-specified time series.

theoreticalFramework: No framework is needed beyond the causal diagram used to choose covariates; the question is a comparison of two policies with routine data.
summary: Cohort of catheters on both sides of the policy change; one primary outcome, two secondary outcomes and one process measure, with clustering and secular trends handled by design.
